what_its_for: Cobimetinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of skin cancer called melanoma that has spread to other parts of your body or cannot be removed by surgery. It is used together with another medicine called vemurafenib (Zelboraf). It only works if your cancer has a specific gene change called a BRAF V600E or V600K mutation, which your doctor will test for before starting treatment.
how_to_take: Take cobimetinib by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablets whole. Try to take your dose at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablets.
dosing: The usual dose is 3 tablets (60 mg total) taken once a day for 21 days in a row. After those 21 days, you stop taking cobimetinib for 7 days. This 28-day cycle (21 days on, 7 days off) then repeats. Your doctor may lower your dose or change your schedule if you have side effects. Always follow exactly what your doctor tells you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. However, if it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store cobimetinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect from moisture and keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use tablets after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (often found in marmalades) while taking this medicine, as they can increase the amount of drug in your body and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher), protective clothing, and sunglasses when outdoors, because this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, especially antifungals, antibiotics, seizure medicines, or St. John's Wort, as many drugs can interact with cobimetinib. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience any of the following: sudden vision changes, blurry vision, or new eye problems; unusual bleeding or bruising; coughing up blood; shortness of breath or new cough; chest pain or a fast or irregular heartbeat; muscle pain, weakness, or dark brown urine (signs of muscle breakdown); severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; new skin growths or changes to existing moles; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; severe diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting; or signs of severe allergic reaction such as difficulty breathing, swelling of face or throat, or severe itching.
when_it_works: Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests, imaging scans, and other check-ups. You may not feel or see any immediate changes when you start treatment. Some patients begin to see results within weeks, but it may take longer. Keep taking your medicine as directed even if you feel well, and do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use cobimetinib if you are pregnant, as it can seriously harm your unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use effective birth control during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 2 weeks after your last dose. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely by their doctor.
